blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 establishes the central banking authority and regulatory foundation.
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 provides comprehensive supervision over commercial banking operations in India.
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 governs financial instruments, including criminal liability for cheque dishonour under Section 138.
The SARFAESI Act, 2002 allows banks and financial institutions to enforce security interests without court intervention.
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) consolidates and amends laws relating to time-bound reorganization and insolvency resolution.

cells: RBI established under RBI Act, 1934; commenced operations 1 April 1935; nationalised 1 January 1949
Issue of bank notes; maintenance of reserves for monetary stability; operating currency and credit system of India
14 Directors + Governor + Deputy Governors (up to 4); Central Board governs RBI
Section 45ZB: 6 members; 3 from RBI + 3 external; fixes policy repo rate; inflation targeting
Section 20: RBI is banker and agent to Central Government; Section 21: also for State Governments
Section 22: Sole right to issue banknotes (except Re.1 note/coin issued by Ministry of Finance)
Section 33: RBI holds gold and foreign securities worth not less than Rs.200 crore (gold not less than Rs.115 crore) against note issue
Section 42: RBI prescribes Cash Reserve Ratio for scheduled banks
Section 17: RBI can make advances to scheduled banks against eligible securities
RBI can impose restrictions on weak banks under PCA Framework

blocks.content: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 is the primary legislation regulating banking companies in India. It gives RBI comprehensive powers to regulate, supervise, and control banks.

cells: Business a banking company may do — banking + permitted businesses
Use of the word 'Bank' — only banking companies can use it
Prohibition on employment of Managing Director with managing agency
Board of Directors: not less than 51% must have professional experience in relevant fields
Requirement of minimum paid-up capital and reserves
Reserve Fund: transfer 20% of profits to statutory reserve every year until it equals paid-up capital
CRR: cash reserve requirement for non-scheduled banks (6% of demand/time liabilities)
Restriction on holding shares in other companies — cannot hold >30% of its own paid-up capital
Restriction on loans and advances to directors, relatives — cannot grant loans to own directors
RBI has power to control advances by banking companies
Licensing of banks: no company can carry on banking business without RBI licence
Branch licensing: opening, closing, shifting of branches requires RBI permission
SLR: maintain Statutory Liquidity Ratio in gold, approved securities, or cash
Return of unclaimed deposits: accounts not operated for 10 years to be reported to RBI
Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF): unclaimed deposits transferred after 10 years
Accounts and balance sheet: every banking company to prepare annually
Inspection of banks by RBI — annual/surprise inspections
Power to give directions: RBI can give directions to any banking company in public interest
Power to acquire undertakings of banking companies (nationalisation power)
Suspension of business and winding up — RBI can apply to High Court
Application to cooperative banks: Chapter V provisions apply to co-op banks

blocks.content: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 governs instruments whose ownership passes by endorsement and delivery (or mere delivery). It defines and regulates promissory notes, bills of exchange, and cheques.

cells: Unconditional promise in writing by maker to pay a certain sum of money to payee; signed by maker
Unconditional order in writing by drawer to drawee to pay a certain sum to payee/order/bearer
Bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker; payable on demand; deemed to be accepted by bank's obligation to honour
Cheque returned unpaid due to insufficiency of funds or if amount exceeds the arrangement with bank
Cheque must be presented within 3 months of date (6 months before 2002 amendment); complaint within 1 month of receiving cause of action
Payee must send written demand notice within 30 days of cheque return information
Drawer must pay within 15 days of receiving notice; failing which, criminal liability arises
Imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both
Metropolitan Magistrate/Judicial Magistrate of First Class having jurisdiction
Under Section 139: court shall presume that cheque was given for legally enforceable debt/liability
Yes — offence can be compounded (settled between parties) at any stage including before High Court
CPC amendment allows trial at place where cheque was drawn or delivered; multiple cheques — one complaint possible
Definition of Cheque; includes electronic image of truncated cheque; electronic cheque
Holder — person entitled in own name to possession and to receive amount
Holder in Due Course — person who takes instrument for value in good faith before maturity without notice of defect
Negotiation by endorsement and delivery; by delivery alone if payable to bearer
Types of Endorsement: Blank, Special/Full, Conditional, Restrictive, Partial, Sans Recours
Liability of drawee of cheque — bank liable if wrongfully dishonours cheque of solvent customer
Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: of consideration, date, time of acceptance, time of transfer, order of endorsements, stamp
Dishonour of cheque; offence and penalties; cognizance

rows: Central banking operations and monetary policy control
Licensing, supervision, and governance of commercial banks
Rules on cheques, bills of exchange, promissory notes, and dishonour remedies
Enforcement of security interest without prior court intervention
Time-bound resolution process for corporate insolvency and bankruptcy

blocks.content: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Securities Interest Act, 2002 allows secured creditors (banks and FIs) to enforce their security interest without court intervention.

cells: Applies to banks, FIs, ARCs for secured debts of Rs.1 lakh and above; not applicable to agricultural land
Account must be classified as NPA; then notices issued under SARFAESI
60-day notice to borrower to repay dues; if failed, secured creditor can proceed
Secured creditor can take possession, sell, appoint manager, or recover income from secured assets
Borrower can approach DRT (Debt Recovery Tribunal) within 30 days of possession notice; deposit 75% of claim first (50% after amendment)
DRT order can be appealed to DRAT (Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal) within 30 days
ARC acquires financial assets from banks at discounted price; must be RBI-registered; issues Security Receipts to Qualified Buyers
Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest; registration of security interests; prevents fraud
Cannot proceed under SARFAESI: agricultural land, loans below Rs.1 lakh, cases under Insolvency Code

blocks.content: 2.5 Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (RDDBFI Act)
The Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 established Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) and Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunals (DRATs) for faster recovery of debts.

cells: Banks and FIs for debts of Rs.20 lakh and above
Quasi-judicial body; presided by Presiding Officer (equivalent to District Judge); application filed by bank
Appellate body against DRT orders; presided by Chairperson (equivalent to HC Judge)
DRT to decide within 6 months; DRAT within 6 months
After adjudication, DRT issues Recovery Certificate; Recovery Officer then attaches and auctions property
75% of amount deposited before DRAT appeal (may be waived by DRAT)
3 years from when debt becomes due; extended in certain circumstances

items: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is heavily tested concerning notice periods and penalties for cheque bounce.
Note the structural differences between debt recovery tribunals under the RDDBFI Act, 1993 and non-judicial enforcement under the SARFAESI Act, 2002.
Memorize the enactment years of major financial acts: RBI Act (1934), BR Act (1949), SARFAESI Act (2002), and IBC (2016).

blocks.content: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is a comprehensive law for resolution of insolvency of individuals, partnership firms, and companies. It consolidates and amends laws relating to insolvency and liquidation.

cells: Time-bound resolution of insolvency; promote entrepreneurship; maximise asset value; balance interests of all stakeholders
NCLT (National Company Law Tribunal) for companies/LLPs; DRT for individuals/partnership firms
NCLAT (National Company Law Appellate Tribunal) for corporate; Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal for others
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India — regulatory body for IPs, IPEs, and information utilities
Manages the insolvency process; registered with IBBI; acts as IRP/RP/Liquidator
Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process: 180 days + 90 days extension = 270 days maximum; 330 days mandatory outer limit (2019 amendment)
Section 14: upon admission of application, moratorium imposed — no suits, no recovery, no asset transfer, no enforcement by secured creditors
Financial creditors form CoC; operational creditors and others do not vote; CoC approves resolution plan by 66% vote
Must provide for full payment of liquidation value to dissenting creditors and operational creditors; minimum payment to operational creditors
If no resolution plan within 330 days; Liquidator appointed; waterfall mechanism for distribution
CIRP costs → Insolvency resolution process costs → Workmen dues (24 months) → Secured creditors → Government dues (2 years) → Unsecured creditors → Equity shareholders
For MSMEs; debtor proposes plan before approaching NCLT; faster; 120 days maximum
Can be proceeded against even if corporate debtor in moratorium; cross-class cramdown possible
For individuals with income < Rs.60,000 and assets < Rs.20,000; discharge of debts
Section 3: Whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or assist in or is party to concealment, possession, acquisition, use, projecting/claiming as untainted property, the proceeds of crime
Section 4: Rigorous imprisonment 3–7 years (up to 10 years for scheduled offences under NDPS Act)
Director ED can provisionally attach property within 180 days; confirmed by Adjudicating Authority
Quasi-judicial body under PMLA; confirms or cancels provisional attachment
PMLA Appellate Tribunal — appeals against Adjudicating Authority orders
Investigates PMLA offences; ED = DRI + Enforcement Directorate; under Ministry of Finance
National agency for receiving/processing financial intelligence; banks must report CTRs, STRs to FIU
All cash transactions above Rs.10 lakh or Rs.10 lakh equivalent in a month must be reported to FIU
Any suspicious transaction regardless of amount must be reported to FIU within 7 days of internal confirmation
Includes: NDPS Act, Arms Act, IPC offences (cheating, forgery, counterfeiting), SEBI violations, cyber crimes under IT Act, corruption, human trafficking
Section 12: Reporting entities must maintain records; identify clients; report to FIU; preserve records for 5 years
Accused must prove property is untainted (reversal of burden of proof — presumption of guilt under Section 24)
